utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I will ask the Registrar to call out the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a-PT, the Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May we have the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If it please your Honours, my name is Niemann and I appear with Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi and Ms. Sutherland for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Toma Fila. I represent the accused, Dokmanovic, and I am assisted here today by Mr. Petrovic and Ms. Lopicic who will join us later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, can you hear me? Thank you. Before we start with the next two witnesses, may I ask the parties whether they have come to some sort of agreement on the admissions? Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have exchanged drafts, but we are still in the process of exchanging drafts. No, we have not reached agreement yet, but we are close to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I received the draft yesterday evening at 7 pm. I have responded to one part of it and I will prepare the remaining part and I believe that by Thursday we will reach an agreement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann, will you call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I call Clyde Snow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, may I ask you whether in light of the acceptance by the admissions by Mr. Fila of a few points in your draft admissions, document of 2nd March, filed on 2nd March 1998, in particular, admissions as to points 7, 10, 11 and 12, whether you are going to confine yourself to asking questions relating to matters which are in dispute so that you will not raise issues which relate to matters which are not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have not reached agreement as yet. There has been an acceptance in part. There has now been a counteroffer which we received this morning to what we proposed yesterday. What had happened is we filed a document last evening. At 5 o'clock we put it in their box. It contained an acceptance of those paragraphs: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7. This morning, we have come back and the Defence have raised other issues, so I am afraid negotiations are still ongoing. I cannot say one way or the other what the outcome will be, but the evidence here today I do not believe will traverse the admissions, but they may well do. Because Dr. Snow is only here today, of course. He then goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Dr. Snow, may I ask you to make the solemn declaration. Could you stand up and read the solemn declaration? DR. CLYDE SNOW (affirmed)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Snow, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Clyde Collins Snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you born in Forth Worth, Texas, in 1928?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you hold an Associate of Arts from New Mexico Military Institute that you received in 1947?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A Bachelor of Science from the Eastern New Mexico University in 1951?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A Master of Science from Texas Technical University in 1955?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A Doctorate of Philosophy, University of Arizona, 1967?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And a degree of science, honours, from the John Jay College of Criminal Justice in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After retiring from a career in the Federal Aviation Administration of the United States of America, have you had a career in forensic science dealing with human skeletal identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During your career, have you served as a consultant in nearly 3,000 cases involving the identification and determination of the cause of death of skeletalised victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do some of the cases that you have been involved in include the 1979 American Airlines DC10 crash in Chicago which claimed the lives of 273 persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The John Wayne Gacy serial murders and the still unresolved Green River murders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1985, at the request of the Simon Wiesenthal Institute, did you head a team of US forensic scientists that went to Brazil in order to identify the skeletal remains of the war criminal Dr. Joseph Mengele?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1984, under the sponsorship of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, did you go to Argentina to serve as a consultant to the National Commission on Disappeared Persons in an effort to determine the fate of thousands of Argentinians who were abducted and murdered by the military death squads between 1976 and 1983?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a result of this investigation, did you testify as an expert witness in the trial of the Junta members who ruled Argentina during the period of military repression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Since then, have you spent nearly one-third of your time on similar missions in Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, Chile, East Salvador, the Philippines, Venezuela, Guatemala, Panama and the Iraqi Kurdistan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1992, did you serve in Geneva as a US delegate to the United Nations Human Rights Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also completed several UN-sponsored missions to the Former Yugoslavia to collect forensic evidence to be used in war crimes trials collected for the Prosecution in the newly then established War Crimes Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In particular, did you become involved in the exhumations of the mass grave at Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you held numerous university appointments, six in number, from the period 1970 to 1983?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you held over 14 consultantships from 1967 through to 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you, in terms of professional organisations, a diplomate of the American Board of Forensic Anthropology?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A Fellow of the American Academy of Forensic Sciences, a Fellow of the American Anthropological Association, a Fellow of the Royal Anthropological Society of Great Britain and Ireland, a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Sciences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: An Associate Current Anthropology, American Association of Physical Anthropologists, Human Biology Council and the Society for the Study of Human Biology?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you held numerous appointments and effective offices from 1973 through to 1994, and have you been given an extensive range of honours from 1970 to 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you participated, organised and directed numerous courses of study from the period 1982 to 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you extensively published and written in this field of study?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look now at the document I show you and can you tell me whether or not this is a correct record of your curriculum vitae? (Handed)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, it is as of March 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender the curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 93, exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Snow, during the year of 1992, were you requested to participate in the examination of a suspected mass grave in the Vukovar area of the Former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell the court the circumstances of how it was that you became involved in that matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, may I refer to my notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the witness refer to his notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have them here. Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court the circumstances of how it is that you became involved with this particular suspected mass grave in Yugoslavia at Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was appointed as a member to the Mazowiecki Commission, a group including some forensic scientists, that was formed by the United Nations and with the mission of coming to the Former Yugoslavia to collect at least preliminary evidence on some of the alleged atrocities that had occurred at that time. My particular mission was to investigate allegations of atrocities involving massacres and clandestine graves and problems within my area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were you approached in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in -- I believe in late September I was first approached to be a member of that commission. It was organised and staged through Geneva and our delegation arrived in Zagreb on October 12th 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What had you learnt about this matter, either prior to arrival or when you arrived in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Concerning the Ovcara case, it was a day or two after we arrived in Zagreb and I , along with Mr. Jack Geiger, the President of the Physicians for Human Rights, who was also a member of the Delegation, we met with Dr. Ivica Kostovic at the medical school. He was the Dean of the Medical Faculty at the time, but also headed up a commission of Croatian experts involved in the identification and the repatriation of war dead during the Croatian-Serbian conflict of 1991. I met with him in his office and he went over several cases, but the one that struck me as being the most interesting was an allegation concerning the around 200 individuals who had gone missing from the hospital in Vukovar on or around November 20th 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when this matter took your interest, what did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I asked -- I asked him for more details and he said that these were individuals who mostly had been patients, many of them wounded during the siege of Vukovar, and also included some male hospital staff and they had been last seen removed in buses from the hospital on the day that -- the morning that Vukovar fell, and that they had never shown up in any kind of an exchange of prisoners that had taken place between the Serbs and the Croats after that. Going over the details, he gave me a map, a topographical map, of the general area of Vukovar which we examined and he also mentioned that there was a witness which -- in these proceedings, who has been referred to as Witness B -- that claimed that he was a survivor of that group and that he was currently residing, not in Zagreb, but in another city I believe close to Zagreb. I indicated I would like to meet this person and hear his story, because the case intrigued me. That was arranged. On the evening of October 15th, Witness B came to my hotel room in the Inter-Continental Hotel in Zagreb and he -- it was room 1405. He got there I think around 6 or 7 o'clock in the evening and in the company in the room was Dr. Geiger and Ms. Lindsay Cook from the Commission, the Mazowiecki Commission, and also as translator, a gentleman named Thomas Osorio. We sat down and, after introductions and making ourselves comfortable, I asked Witness B to tell his story, just right from the beginning to the end, and I wanted him to tell that more or less without interruptions and then I would go back over details with him after he had told -- narrated his account.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Snow, you said that you had a topographical map with you at the time that you had obtained during the course of your stay in Zagreb. Would you look at the document now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: (Handed). Is this a copy of the map that you had on the particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, this is a copy and it is a map, 1:25,000 scale, produced in 1973. It shows the area of -- around the little farming village of Ovcara, which is a few kilometres south and west of the city of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Snow, you said that you had asked this Witness B to recount uninterrupted his story. Are you able to recall now what he told you on that particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, in general I can. He told me that he was -- had been slightly wounded in the siege of Vukovar. He had been a member of the Croatian Defence Forces and although he was not a hospitalised patient at the time, he had -- he went up to the hospital that morning because he heard that the patients from the hospital were going to be evacuated back to Croatian-held territory. So he was up there at the time the Serb forces organised this evacuation of the male -- more or less the walking wounded -- the people who were still ambulatory -- and told them to load themselves on a series of buses that had pulled into the back of the hospital. So he was loaded on to one of those buses and then they proceeded to a military post on the outskirts of Vukovar, there are some barracks as I believe, and they stayed there for several hours, and then later in the afternoon, they were taken out to the village of Ovcara. There they were offloaded from the buses and went into a barn or a hangar-like building where, for another few hours, they were threatened and brutalised in some cases by their captors. He said that about dark or a little after dark, the captors started organising them into groups of around 20 prisoners and that a truck would pull up to the building and they would load a group of 15 to 20 men on to the truck and then in about 15 minutes later, 15 to 20 minutes later, the truck would return empty. It was always the same truck, as he recalled, and he would -- they would take another load of prisoners. So he assumed from watching what was going on that the round trip of the truck was taking about 15 to 20 minutes. As I recall, he believed that he was boarded on the third or fourth truck. I should point out that I am recalling this after several years and he has probably given testimony. If there are minor discrepancies, I would go with his version because it was probably a much more vivid experience for him, but I think he said it was the third or fourth truck that he was loaded on. By this time, he was fairly apprehensive. He felt like something bad was happening out there. So he got -- when he boarded, he was toward the back of the truck that he was on and he said that the truck left Vukovar and went down an improved road that leads to another village called Grabovo, I believe, a few kilometres south and west of Ovcara. After about a kilometre, the truck left that road and made a left turn into a -- on to a dirt road that was bordered on the right, as the truck was travelling, by trees and on the left, by open fields. So he said that he jumped out of the rear of the truck and started running and he ran towards his left, across the open fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Snow, just to interrupt, sorry to interrupt you, but you said a moment ago that the truck left Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. I meant Ovcara. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you: you were at the point where you said that he jumped out of the rear of the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said he jumped out of the rear of the truck and started running and I asked him, did he see anything or hear anything? He said, well, he was running and running away from the truck, back in the general direction of Vukovar and he did hear or thought he heard the truck stop a few moments after he jumped out of the truck and he heard some scattered gunshots and he felt like -- that perhaps another prisoner had also made an attempt to escape, but this time it was noticed that perhaps the truck had stopped and they were firing at another escapee. That was his theory. It was the only way he could account for the handful of shots that he heard. I asked him if he had seen anything else. Did he hear any cries or screams? Did he hear more gunshots? Enough to execute a truckload of individuals? He said no. He said that he was running so hard that he did not hear anything, he did not see anything. He eventually made his way back to Vukovar where, I believe the next morning, he surrendered to a Yugoslavian National Army group and was later repatriated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he told you this story, did you have the map with you that has now been marked as exhibit 94?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were any markings placed on the map during the course of this discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, I made -- talking to him, he is an engineering officer by the way and I think a civil engineer by profession, so he is pretty familiar with topographical maps and we looked at the map there, and the only area where the terrain matched his description is a ravine that runs across the Ovcara/Grabovo Road about a kilometre from Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, just so that we can show it to the court, I would ask, with the assistance of the usher, whether this map could be placed on the overhead projector beside you there and I will ask you some questions about the map. Just looking at the map -- we will have to wait until it comes up on the screen. (Pause). It does not seem as though it is going to work, so we will have to do it the hard way. We may have some action here. Yes, there we are. Dr. Snow, could you just to assist us, can you point to the place written as Ovcara on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, right here is the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And Grabovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the ravine that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ravine crosses this road between Ovcara and Grabovo at this point. It is the area shown in green here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the circle that appears to be written in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. That was where I , after talking to Witness B, and looking at the terrain, we agreed that this had to be the area that he had seen as the truck was proceeding this way, an area with timber on his right and open fields on his left. At that time, I put a small dot on the map because my theory and my experience in this sort of thing is that this would be the area where one would put a mass grave. For one reason, it is not only my experience in dealing with mass graves, but, having been raised out in Texas and Oklahoma, I know that farmers and ranchers generally consider the head of a ravine like this as sort of wasteland. That is where you put any junk you have on the farm. As a means of controlling, helping control erosion from the surrounding fields. Certainly no good farmer is going to allow a mass grave to be put in a very productive cornfield or grain field, so I just made this little point close to the head of the ravine here and then drew a larger circle around it and I said I thought that maybe the grave would have been in this general area, thinking that the truck probably proceeded out up into this field for a while after Witness B jumped from the truck and perhaps they stopped there to offload the prisoners. If indeed they were executing these prisoners, then it would be in this general area. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you get a sense from Witness B about where along that ravine he in fact jumped from the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This distance from where the ravine crosses a road up to the top of the road is about 0.9 kilometres. As I recall he said 2 or 300 kilometres after the truck turned into the field was where he made his jump, so that would put it in this area along in here somewhere. Because you have to remember it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think when you say "kilometres", you mean metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 300 metres, yes. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after you had had this discussion with Witness B and the point was marked on the map, what was the next thing that you did in relation to this alleged mass grave at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I informed the members of the Commission of my findings or the results of the interview and it was determined -- they asked if I would make my way over there and explore this area in a little more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you been there before this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I flew over with some other Commission members to Belgrade, arriving there, I believe, on October 16th and then the next day, I went, along with a driver, over to Vukovar. There at Vukovar I contacted the UN authorities there. Not in Vukovar, but in what was serving as more or less the headquarters for the UN, Erdut, at the post at Erdut. There I met a Royal or a Canadian military policeman, Staff Sergeant Larry Moore. He had been stationed there for several months, by that time, I believe, and he was fairly familiar with the area. I showed him the map and we decided to go out there and explore this place. So on the next morning, the 18th, Sergeant Moore and I and Ms. Vlandina Nega, who was a civilian Affairs Officer in Sector East there at the time, and a General Peeters, then Colonel Peeters, who was the Commander of the Belgian battalion in Sector East, and his adjutant or at least one of his staff officers. So we proceeded out to the site. When we got there, the road -- there had been some rain in the area so we parked our vehicles at -- along the main road and at the bridge here (indicating) where the road crosses this little ravine and started walking up in this direction. As we walked up the field through the mud, I think Ms. Nega and I , we lagged a little further behind and Sergeant More was in the lead and he got up to the -- toward the top of the ravine. I told him to look for anything suspicious in the form of the site disturbed or if there are other features that would suggest some disturbance in the area after a year. We were perhaps a couple of hundred metres behind Sergeant More when he started shouting and asking us to come on up and we went up there and he was standing at an area right at the head of the ravine there that did look -- give some indications of disturbance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was that place consistent with the area that you had marked with the circle on your map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very close to -- it is well within the circle. It is actually very close to the little dot inside the -- I think within about 20 or 30 metres. Never measured it, but rather close to our point of prediction, you might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have a camera with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you take a number of slides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took some slides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you have those slides with you in court today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in order to explain your evidence, would you like to refer to those slides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And if your Honours please, may we tender these slides now and uplift them to have them copied so that Dr. Snow can take his original slides back with him? Your Honours, we will undertake to do that after his evidence and provide the court with photographs of the slides, if that pleases the court. I tender the map that is now before you, the map that you had had marked --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 94.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, referring to the slides, firstly, Dr. Snow, would you just briefly cast your eye over this document I now show you and can you tell me if it accurately depicts an index to the slides that you are about to refer to in your evidence? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, it has -- it is a brief index of 28 slides showing the general subject of each slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender the index, your Honour, of the slides.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, Dr. Snow, during the course of your testimony, when you are referring to a particular slide, can you refer to the number, the slide number, that is shown on the index that is now exhibit 95, so that we can keep track of which particular slide you are referring to in your evidence? Your Honours, if it please the court, I will tender the slides as one exhibit, reference to them being through this index rather than individually marking each slide, so, if that pleases the court, it may be a more efficient and easier way to do it, especially for the Registrar who would have to otherwise mark each one individually. Dr. Snow, having regard to the slides that you took on the particular occasion and on a later occasion, can you now proceed to describe what you saw when you arrived at this site? You were at the point in your evidence where you said that Sergeant More had reached a point and was waving and indicating to you that he had found something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir. Are we going to show these slides, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, with the assistance of the usher, perhaps they could be placed on the ELMO, and if we put them on a particular spot on the ELMO that is marked, we should be able to see them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to remember to refer to the slide numbers, counsellor, but if I forget to do that, I am sure I can count on you to remind me. This is slide no. 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just waiting for it to come up. Having some trouble with the ELMO today, it seems. Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, I am not sure how it is showing up on your video there, but on mine, this is a little out of focus. Is there any way we can tighten up the focus?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think this is about as good as it is going to get.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is slide number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is slide no. 1 and this shows Sergeant More standing in the area that had attracted his attention and what he is looking at there is an area where there are a number of weeds in there that look like they are only about one year's growth. They had not been growing there a long time, as opposed to some larger trees and saplings around the area. So he waited for us and I will show slide no. 2 now. Can we raise that slide just a bit? He is still standing there, but we are a little different angle. You can see a cleared area out here with some puddles of water in it and it is obvious that that area has been subject to some disturbance during the past few months or a year or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is slide no. 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is slide no. 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And can you just perhaps explain to us why this area was something that attracted your attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because usually in mass graves, when the soil is disturbed, it takes at least a few years for normal vegetation to come back and cover the area, so this is -- one of the hallmarks, the diagnostic signs, of a mass grave is evidence of -- surface evidence of disturbance from not only the earth itself, but the surrounding vegetation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, as we walked into the area, Sergeant More, who had some concern about mines, insisted on going in first, followed by myself and Colonel Peeters and the rest of our party. As we walked into the area, one of the things that immediately caught my eye was that on the surface here, here is a human skull beginning to -- is partially exposed and I do not know whether we have a fine enough pointer that I can point this out on the slide or not, but it is right in the centre of the slide, a little to the left there. You can see the two eye sockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is this photograph taken in the condition that you found it or had you removed some of the soil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point, that was more or less in the condition we found it. I did not do any cleaning. It was more or less in that same position or same condition. If I could show --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is slide no. 3, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is slide no. 3 and slide no. 4 is a close up. Here, to get you oriented, you can see the skull itself, the cranial vault, the brain portion of the skull is up here in the upper centre of the slide. Down towards your left, you can see a socket here, an eye socket, and a nose and perhaps some of the jaw bones, some teeth showing here. So the skull is facing left and we are looking at its left side, more or less in profile. Even at that point, one of the things that I was struck by was right in the centre of the slide there, on the left side of the skull and just behind the eye socket is a darkened defect there and that was indeed a hole in the skull about, as I recall, 2 centimetres square and with a fracture or two radiating out from its margins and going up into the substance of the skull itself. Looking at it, just there in that position, I could see some of the bevelling on the surface, the margins of the hole, that is characteristic of what we see when a bullet exits the skull, so it had, to me, the characteristics of an exit wound. In other words, back over behind here, we would expect to find the entrance wound where the bullet entered the skull and then passed out from the -- just behind the eye socket over here on the left side of the skull.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are looking at photograph no. 4 in exhibit 95?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what happened after you had seen -- made this discovery? What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then I -- we walked back over the immediate area of disturbed earth, about 15 metres from the grave in a little ravine close to the grave itself, or to this area. At that time, I was not willing to definitely diagnose it as a grave, but we found another skeleton and more or less on the surface of the ground. The bones had been bleached white like they had been exposed to the sun for a while, as bones will do with sun exposure. Some of the bones had been damaged by animal scavengers. The ends had been gnawed off by perhaps feral wild dogs, or some sort of a medium-sized animal or animals had attacked the bone and there was a little bit of clothing. At that point, we had seen evidence of two individuals on or near the surface of that grave. As we walked back, we also noticed that there was some evidence of -- in the trees, on one side of the grave, there were actually holes that looked like bullet holes, some of them penetrating some of the small saplings immediately behind the grave. As we walked back through the area, I also saw another sign of perhaps another individual just a scapula or a shoulder blade lying on the ground, and so this entire visit did not take more than 15 or 20 minutes. It was enough to convince me that this site was worthy of further investigation and we were also extremely concerned about the security of the site at that point, because down in the ravine, as we had walked up, there were a couple of vehicles there that I recall, a tractor and a wagon, and there were some men in the woods, apparently chopping wood. We knew that if they observed our activities out there, the word would spread very rapidly that perhaps we had found this grave and so we left the scene. We went back to Erdut and, as it turned out, the area around Ovcara was in the jurisdiction of the Russian battalion, which I believe with the Belgium battalion had responsibility for that area of Sector East. We arranged for Russian battalion troops to go out and secure this scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just stopping you for a moment there, Dr. Snow, the skeletal remains that you examined on the site there on the first occasion, did you make any determination, preliminary or otherwise, at the time as to the sex and possible age of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looking at that skull and looking at the -- that was on the surface there, I could pretty well tell that it was a male, probably a young adult male, and with evidence of a gunshot wound and roughly from the little time I had looking at the skeleton that was lying in the woods, I could also determine that it was that of probably a young adult male, but I did not have time to do a detailed examination at that point. The scene security seemed a matter of priority then. So, conferring back in Erdut, we explained that this was -- we would have to consider it a homicide site and so it should be secured like any other crime scene and kept under security until a proper investigation could be mounted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I just want to stop you again before we get into that. You said that you looked at some trees behind the grave site to see whether or not there would be any bullet holes, and indeed you did discover some. What made you look in that particular spot and what caused you to look at that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We happened to be in that particular area because, as we had explored around the grave, that skeleton, it was on the surface, attracted our attention, so when we walked back in that area, we looked at some of the trees and, sure enough, there was what appeared to be bullet marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sorry, I interrupted you. You were saying how you had made a determination at Erdut that this should be secured. What was done about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- our first arrangement was that the Russian troops or soldiers, it would take them three or four hours to get organised and get out to the scene. In the meantime, Sergeant More sent a couple of his people over, as I recall, and they parked out there until around I think it was -- the Russian -- there was a little confusion there because the Russian troops had trouble finding the scene and I do not believe that they actually arrived out there until around 11 pm and then they took over from Sergeant Moore's people and there was one other difficulty. We went out again the next morning to look around and the Russian troops had left and they had -- there had been a misunderstanding. They thought that this was only a one night stand, if you will. They had left there around 10 o'clock in the morning, so we had to go back in again and explain that this was -- the security would have to be maintained 24 hours a day from that point until the investigation was completed, no matter how long it took. So they were sent back out and they set up a permanent station. They laid some concertina wire around the grave site and it was put under full security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, the Russians maintained the site from then in 1992 right up until the point where UNTAES took over the site; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, that would be July of 1996, as I recall, July or August, somewhere in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after this visit in October of 1992, what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Mazowiecki Commission, we returned to Geneva and they issued their report, with part of that small annex describing my findings at Ovcara. Then about a month later, I went back with Mr. Eric Stover, who that time was the Executive Director of Physicians for Human Rights. They were working with the Commission, and Dr. Becky Saunders, an archaeologist that I had worked with before in Guatemala, and also Dr. Morris Tidball-Binz from Argentina who at that time was working with Amnesty International, and I had worked with him a number of years in our investigation -- a number of years before in our investigations in Argentina. I should point out Dr. Binz is no longer with Amnesty International. He is down with the Inter-American Court in Costa Rica at this point. But we returned --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was about 17th December, was it? I think you said a month later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly a month later. Actually, a little later than that. I think our returned to Ovcara was on December 17th and so we went back out to the site and I have some more slides now, if we could continue the slide presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps the lights could be dimmed. I think it makes it easier to see the slides. Is this slide no. 5 in exhibit 95?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is slide no. 5, counsel. This is an aerial view of the site. Actually, this slide was taken about a month or two months later when we made a third visit to the site, which I will describe a little later. But it shows the general area of the Vukovar grave and over here on the left, toward the centre of the slide is a vehicle and a small trailer house that the Russian troops occupied. The weather in that area being very severe, they needed some shelter. You may be able to see over here toward the right of the slide a large tree and then around the periphery, I believe the concertina wire shows up, and enclosed in that area is the area that we are interested in, the open area there toward the bottom of the slide, but just above the concertina wire is the area that we were particularly interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I think there is a date shown there on the exhibit 95. It says 17/19th December. That is wrong, is it? That date? See on the index?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let us see what I did with the index. It says 17th to 19th December.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said this slide was taken a bit later; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This slide was taken in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: March of what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the same year, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I showed the slide even though it is not in chronological order here because it shows the general topography and aerial view of the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, continue on, if you will.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will take this next slide, which should be slide no. 6. This just shows the party that we brought out for this preliminary -- we called it a reconnaissance or exploration of the site -- in December. Standing farthest to the left there, the gentleman in the blue jacket is Dr. Morris Tidball-Binz. The woman in the green jacket is Dr. Becky Saunders and then I am standing there more or less in profile, and right behind me is one of the CIVPOL officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The grave site, that is on the other side of the wire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The grave site is on the other side of the wire at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is photograph no. 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In exhibit 95. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this is just a shot taken from within the grave area. You can see the -- looking more or less north, the concertina wire and the vehicle used by the Russian troops for their rotation, daily rotation, and behind that is the Russian guard shack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is photograph no. 7 on exhibit 95?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir. This is myself and over to the left there -- myself over to the left there and Dr. Becky Saunders in the centre of the picture, and we are standing in the area of the grave, the open area of disturbance, and you can see that there had been some rain there and we had a large puddle of muddy water and we had to make some -- a little drainage ditch to drain that off so that we could work under drier conditions. That took a while. I should also add that, among other signs, in addition to the visual disturbance that you see in this site, there are also olfactory signs. There is an odour of decomposition very commonly associated with these places and that was certainly apparent there, that something had been -- some sort of animals had been buried in this grave. From what we could see from the surface, human skeletons -- the bodies that were buried there would have to be human.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is photograph no. 8 in exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We walked through the area looking for any signs of disturbance. Had anybody been out between the time of -- had been there the previous October and now a couple of months later, had there been any attempts to disturb the grave? There were none. There were no signs of disturbance, with one exception. I am looking down there at this first skull that we saw, that is more or less at my feet now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is photograph no. 9 of exhibit 95?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It had been cleaned off and some of the mud removed from around the surface of the skull and perhaps the skull had been repositioned a little bit. I was curious about that and I found out that a British medical officer had heard about this find a couple of days after we were there in October, and he took it on himself to go out and make a brief examination of the skull that was found. But aside from that, that was the only evidence that we had that there had been any attempts to tamper with the grave. In other words, the Russian detachment apparently had done their work pretty well. Could I show the next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. We are looking at slide no. 10 in exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once we got the area drained out a little bit so we could work, we started laying it out and gritting it as we would any archaeological site, putting down stakes and strings. Here is Dr. Tidball-Binz driving a stake in there, and so that we would have the general parameters of the grave grit so that it would enable us to give better locational data in our subsequent investigation and mapping and thing of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Slide no. 11 of exhibit 95?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the general area of the grave. It is enclosed now by a string and rectangles. We found our estimate was that at that time, from what we could see, within this boundary, that the grave itself, there were signs of soil disturbances and the grave itself was around 10 metres long and about 7 metres wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to make any assessment as to how it had been dug?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My impression was, and this was shared by Dr. Saunders, the archaeologist, that most likely this grave showed a sort of a regular rectangularity that would make it consistent at least with having been scooped out with a bulldozer or some kind of heavy equipment. It did not show -- usually graves that are say hand dug by shovels tend to be circular. Their boundaries are less distinct, more irregular, so that was our impression at the time, that this was done with some machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. You are going on to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once we had laid out that larger grid enclosing the perimeter of the grave, our next stage was to do -- open what we had referred to as an exploratory trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are now looking at photograph no. 12 on exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. So -- we did not have the time or the manpower of course to do a full exhumation, which we realised would take much more time and many more people, but we did want to establish the fact that this was indeed a mass grave with humans inside and in addition to these two bodies or two skeletons that we found on the surface. So we laid out a 1 metre trench spanning the breadth of the grave, the grave being around, as I said, about 7 metres wide, so this cut across the trench would be about the same width as the grave and about a metre wide. You can see the two strings outlining the boundaries of this projected exploratory trench. We also had some military people there from the Belgian battalion and they were concerned about the possibility of mines or booby-traps, so before we started doing any digging, they went over the area as well as they could with their mine-detectors to make sure that it was safe enough to do some digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now looking at photograph no. 13 of exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir. Once we had laid out the boundaries of that trench, we began removing the top layer of soil and that is fairly heavy work, but the members of the Russian battalion, those boys had been standing out there for a couple of months at that time and they were getting pretty bored and so they very enthusiastically helped us in removing the initial topsoil. It was bitterly cold that day so I think they kind of looked forward to a little physical activity and this shows them beginning the exploration or removal of the topsoil from the trench. Once we got down around -- it varied from one point to another in the trench, but roughly in the range of around 10 to 20 centimetres down below the surface -- we began to encounter human remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are now looking at photograph No. 14 of exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We saw -- as I said before, we did not want to remove these bodies at this point. We just wanted to get a general impression of the number of bodies that might be in this small area and that in fact they were indeed human bodies. So, as we worked along that trench, we began to expose signs of human bodies. For example, this individual you can see a sleeve. It is a right arm and the hand is still somewhat flesh-covered and so he is lying more or less across the trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just by looking at that, were you able to -- and from your experience -- make any assessment as to how long that body may have been there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point, my impression was that it could be anywhere from a few months to perhaps a year or, you know, 6 to 18 months or something in that range. It was certainly the condition of the bodies that we saw was consistent with the -- what we were told about the incident at Ovcara, that these bodies -- these people had been placed in the mass grave on or around November 20th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next slide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This shows further progress of the work along the trench. In fact, it is almost at the end of the exploratory trench or the exploration. In this stretch of roughly 7 metres across, we encountered 9 bodies, 9 separate individuals, laying in one position or another so that either their feet or their hands or sometimes the whole body fell within that area that we had limited by the trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are looking at photograph number 15 in exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that brought us up to, including the two bodies that we found on the surface, we could say that at least 11 people had been buried in this area and we suspected many more. As I indicated before, we did not remove the bodies. We just looked at what we saw as each one surfaced along the stretch of the trench. Then, when we were finished, we refilled the trench as carefully as we could and laid plastic sheets down over the exposed bodies so that they would be protected from the earth that we were going to use to recover them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you were out there, did you draw a sketch of the scene, both showing the grave site itself and then showing the trench that was dug?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, we did. I will have to apologise for the quality of the slide. In fact, besides that, we have it upside down. This is a rough map or sketch map showing the approximate boundaries of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are now looking at photograph number 16 of exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The direction of the map: north would be towards your left here. In other words, roughly this trench is running not exactly, but more or less, north and south. The trench is the horizontal band that you see running across the grave area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Snow, I think we have a hard copy of this slide and if you could put that on the ELMO and point to it with your pointer and I hand it to the usher here. Might that be marked and then given to Dr. Snow? Because you cannot point out things on the slides because they are too small on the ELMO, you may be able to use this enlarged version of the same slide, which might be given the next number in order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is 96.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you would be so kind, I think it is the next page is the one that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you can use the pointer now on the ELMO, you can point to the various markings there on the that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, here is the exploratory trench and, indicated within it, these are body -- portions of body that were exposed as we opened that trench. For example, I believe this feature right here is the arm we were looking at in the slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are now looking at exhibit 96.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The boundaries here are fracture lines in the soil itself. When graves like this are made and covered, as they begin to subside, you will find that the earth itself fractures. You will see little cracks in the earth that more or less run along the boundaries of the grave and so these were the lines of those fractures as we saw them on the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You are now pointing to the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. Right along here and along here, this being our trench, (indicating), this being the right arm that I showed in the slide. Up here is the skeleton of the individual whose skull I noted on that first visit and out here in this area were the remains of the second individual's. Out away from the grave space a little bit. To this day, I am not sure how he managed -- this body got into this area. It could have been that he was executed later and just after the grave was made and left on the side or died later or it could be that, as we have seen in other cases, where people -- wounded -- actually managed to get out of a grave like this and crawl off a little way and then die or hopefully maybe even escape. So this is the map. Any further questions about the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While we are at it, perhaps the other hard copy, you might explain that to us while you are there. If you could have the second page of exhibit 96, which is in fact the first page as it appears.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a larger view of the area. North is roughly this way and west back toward the east. The open area that we saw in here, these are the areas of heavy vegetation and small trees, and it was this open area here that excited our attention and which is shown in more detail on this map. Here is the road more or less parallel to this band of timber lining this ravine here, and this area up here would be the head or the top of the ravine. The area up here is cultivated fields, so this is just an enlargement. It does show where we found the first skeleton at this end of the area of disturbed earth and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is marked as SSK1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, this is a little ravine that leads away from the grave and fairly heavily wooded. This area is where we found the remains of the second skeleton.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Marked SSK2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Continuing on with the slides that you have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe this will be slide --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Number 17?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 17 of exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will apologise for the quality of this slide. The lighting conditions out there that day were not very good, but among other things we observed was: out on the surface of the grave area itself and particularly along its margins were signs of spent cartridges, and this indeed shows one of those; this arrow here is pointing toward it. It does not show up too well on the slide, but we found a number of those in the general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Photograph 18?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not -- at that time, since this was an exploratory effort -- want to collect any of the evidence, but we did mark the points with these little red flags here where we found spent cartridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They are in the foreground, are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are in the foreground here and close to the boundary of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are looking at photograph 18 of exhibit 95. Dr. Snow, these cartridges, did you then or subsequently make any assessment or determination as to what ammunition they related to or what ammunition they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were -- I am not a ballistics expert, but they appeared to be all -- or at least the majority that we found -- and this by the way is not all; we were only able to flag the ones that were obviously on the surface; later on, many more were found -- but that they were fired from an AK47, the general calibre and the type of ammunition used in that particular firearm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. The next photograph? Photograph 19 of exhibit 95?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here are two of the UNPROFOR people from BelBat, the same people that did the de-mining out there with us and, as I indicated before, as you cross and go to the far side of the area, down close to that little ravine where we found the second skeleton, we had noticed that there were a number of bullet marks in trees and some of them -- for example, I believe in this small sapling here, the bullet passed all the way through the branch of the tree. He is putting a pointer through the bullet hole and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the pointer immediately above the red ribbon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And so several of those were noted. Our general impression was that whoever was firing the ammunition, that because the AK47 tends to eject usually about 10 to 15 feet to the right of the shooter, that most of those spent cartridge cases that we found on the ground out there were more or less on the corner of the grave that would be south and west, close to the south-west corner of the grave, and that that they were firing more or less diagonally. The trajectory was predominantly more or less diagonal across the grave surface itself, so they were standing perhaps close to the north-west corner and firing generally toward the south-east corner. That could be made a little clearer if I could refer to the map again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, if you would like to do that. Perhaps you might go back to exhibit 96. It might be easier to do that on exhibit 96 using the pointer. Just looking at the second page of exhibit 96, the sketch shown of the grave site there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here is generally north in this direction. (Indicated). The concentration of cartridge cases were over in this area, actually kind of off this particular map, and the saplings that had been pierced by bullets were over in this area, so it was our impression that perhaps the shooters, since the cartridge cases would be ejected to their right, that the shooters were down in this corner and perhaps firing more or less diagonally across the grave from here to up in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would be slide number 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, this is after we had done the -- completed our exploratory trench, I returned to the skeleton no. 1 and examined it a little more carefully than I did in that first very hasty visit a couple of months before. Here is the skull in the centre of your screen there, and again right behind that black blob that is the eye-hole, the left eye-hole, you see another sort of square defect there in the left temple area and some fracture lines radiating out from that. Examining the skull in more detail, I felt like we were dealing with a young male in his early 20s, not only from the skull, but the other bones of the skeleton that we were able to examine. Indeed, it will not show it on any of these slides, but over on the right side of the skull, right up in about this area is a very small circular entrance wound, so we could tell that the bullet traversed from the right, exiting over to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next slide, no. 21 of exhibit 95?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, although we were under pretty difficult field conditions, we took that skeleton that was on the surface and cleaned it up and I took some preliminary measurements. For example, here I am measuring a femur or a thighbone, and from that we could develop an estimate of this person's stature, his height in life. That, with other observations made on the other bones, I was able to come up with my estimates of the person's age, his height. I think I was able from the bones that we saw at that time, to determine whether he was left or right-handed and looked for other signs of trauma that might have been inflicted at or about the time of his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Next slide, slide no. 22 of exhibit 95?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, with that particular skeleton, we were able to find some clothing and some items of personal effects or jewellery. They do not show up too well here, but the pointer, right below the card there, the pointer is coming down to the more or less centre and it is pointing to a small gold chain that we found that had a small square -- sort of good luck medal it looks to me like. It looked to me like a four-leaf clover and then a rectangular medal with the inscription which was translated for me as "God and Croatia". Can I take the next slide which will be slide number --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 23, referred to in exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here is a close-up of that and there is a crucifix on your left. I said, I believe -- I said that was a gold chain. It was not a gold chain. It was some sort of silver metal chain. In the centre there is this small square and this was a gold ornament and over on your right is the medallion that says in Croatian, "God and Croatia". I was told at the time that this kind of a medallion was very often worn by persons in the Croatian forces during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next one, photograph 24 referred to in exhibit 95?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is our skeleton no. 2 and it shows some of the bones lying in association with the clothing. You can see the bones are not complete. There is a humerus or an upper arm bone lying diagonally across the centre there, but the ends have been gnawed away by animals. Down in the lower left is a rib. The bones have been scattered and disturbed, but the clothing was still there and -- may I show the next slide?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Slide 25 referred to in exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And again, looking at the skeleton as best we could under field conditions, for example, I am holding up the bones of the pelvis here, the two hip bones, and from their general shape and configuration, I could again determine that this individual was a male, and, from the configuration of the joint between those two hip bones where they meet in front of the body, the age. There are some age indicators there that told me again that we were dealing with a young male in his 20s.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Next slide in exhibit 95, slide number 26.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With this second skeleton, it says "Surface Skeleton 2" there, we found a garment that appeared to be like a jersey, a little heavier than a T-shirt, like a sweatshirt, and it had this inscription on it, the word "Canadian", and I no longer recall the wording of the line under it. But we thought that was significant because we had been told that during the siege of Vukovar a shipment of clothes had been sent from Canada and that it had been -- a lot of it consisted of clothing that -- like T-shirts or sweatshirts and things of that sort -- that would naturally have some sort of a Canadian connection. We were told that many of the items of clothing were passed out to the hospital patients, so, as tenuous as it was, it did suggest that this person had received that clothing in the clothing donated by whatever Canadian relief organisation it was. Also, in one of the pockets of another garment --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are looking at photo 27 of exhibit 95?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are looking at a small religious medal here -- Roman Catholic religious medal -- that was found in the clothing of skeleton number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Finally, photograph number 28 referred to in exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 28. After we finished our work there, we left the scene as close to how we found it as possible. As I indicated before, we recovered the trench, and also before we left we took skeleton no. 1 and no. 2 and put them in separate plastic bags and we buried them at the end of this trench and marked the note -- noted their exact location of burial. I was concerned if it was several months or several years before a proper exhumation or full exhumation could be launched, that these bones would become scattered or picked up or disturbed, so we thought it was better to go ahead and bag them up, put them back in our -- put them in this trench so that they could be found later and would be in a good state of preservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after the break, your Honour, I will ask Dr. Snow to assemble the slides in the condition and order in which they are shown in exhibit 95 before I tender them. Does your Honour wish to take the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We stand in recess for 20 minutes. (10.55 am) (A short adjournment) (11.15 am)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender the slides, all as one exhibit if I may. As I indicated earlier, I would seek to uplift them and have them copied. Perhaps they could be given the next exhibit number in order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The slides will be exhibit no. 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. After you had been at this site in December of 1992, Dr. Snow, did you then subsequently return to the site for a short period in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And who did you return with on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was after the investigation had become moved under the auspices of -- I believe they call it the Commission of Experts -- we made a further visit to the site, a very brief one, in the company of Commander Fenrick from the Canadian -- I am not sure what they call it -- in Canada we call it the judge advocate's office in the military in the US. And one of his colleagues, also a military lawyer from Canada, a Major or Captain Carter and Eric Stover, again, the Executive Director of Physicians for Human Rights and some other people who I really could not recall their names at this point, but we were the principals of that particular group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What had you in mind on that occasion when you had gone back to the site in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had intended to just make a brief walk through from the site to familiarise Commander Fenrick and Major Carter -- I believe he was a major -- with the general layout of the area and it was going to be -- it was planned as a very brief visit so that they could become familiar with the physical aspects of the site, the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. And then did you go back to the site on yet another occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My last visit to the site was in 1996 when the principal excavation began, but in October of 1993, I was -- we put together a team which -- at that time we intended to do the full exhumation, but before we could really deploy and begin the work, they were forced to undeploy, and -- after they had been out there for the first day or so -- and I had not joined the party at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was the Commission of Experts, Commander Fenrick and company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and a team of a number of scientists that we had recruited from PHR.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You did not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Physicians for Human Rights, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Although you did not attend there at the time yourself, you were in the vicinity or nearby, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was over at a place called Pakracka Poljan which is in Croatia and I am not sure of the exact distance from the Ovcara site, but it was out of Sector East.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you hear why Commander Fenrick and his team did not carry out the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time our team or the work was interrupted they received a threat of violence by some of the local people in the Vukovar area, some of the people on the City Council. I am not sure which political body it was. They felt like -- the UN people that were providing us with security at the time thought that on the basis of whatever threat they received, they would not be able to guarantee the security of scientists and the integrity of the work that would proceed, so we pulled up stakes and moved back to the area of Pakracka Poljan. The intended work at Vukovar or at Ovcara was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At some stage, did you get involved in the establishment of an ante mortem database?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was much later in 1996, the autumn -- late summer and autumn of 1996 -- when we finally were able to deploy a full team of scientists and begin to initiate the exhumation of the remains at Ovcara, and this was under the direction of the Tribunal and again, cooperating with the Physicians for Human Rights. As the bones of the bodies were removed, they were taken to Zagreb where we had set up a morgue for their detailed examination by pathologists and anthropologists and other specialists in this area and the project -- the portion of the project that I undertook was to set up a database that we could use to help in the identification of the victims. Now, actually, the roots of that database go back to the very first visits during the Mazowiecki Commission, where, after briefly talking to Dr. Kostovic, I met some of his personnel and staff involved in the project of repatriation and identification of remains from the Serbo-Croatian conflict and I helped them set up the skeleton of the -- the skeletal plan of the database. At that time, they had a little more than lists of names and perhaps birth dates of people who had disappeared and had not been accounted for in the Vukovar area at the time, and these names had come from several sources. One -- a Croatian Red Cross had a list. Amnesty International had a second list. I believe the International Commission, the Red Cross, had a third list. Many of the names were duplicates, so we started by reading those out and we finally came up with a list of roughly, as I recall, around 330 people who at that time in 1992 had not been accounted for. Later, working again on the subsequent visits, each time I would go back to -- each time I returned, I spent some time with the people working on this database and I helped them get started on collecting the kind of information that we would need to establish these identifications, stating not only the name of the person, their age, but from interviews with relatives, family members, from medical or dental records, trying to get a physical description of these people in terms of their stature, other features we could determine with a fair degree of reliability from the skeleton, for example, whether they are right-handed or left-handed, do they have any history of old injuries such as fractures or operations that would show up or other medical conditions that might show up on the skeleton. Anything in addition that we could collect on their dental status, whether they had -- another area of interest in setting up the database -- with the kinds of injuries, particularly the hospital patients, the kinds of injuries they had suffered in the siege of Vukovar, because these we felt would show up as wounds that would be apparent on the body when the pathologists were doing the examination, or perhaps X-rays as we examined the bodies. So as complete a physical description of the person that we could find. At the same time, we were working on other aspects of the database. For example, that number I recall as being about 330 people that we started out with in 1992, that was being progressively whittled down as more and more people were accounted for as perhaps living -- still alive and living elsewhere. During all of the confusion, their relatives had lost track of them and reported them missing. Also, some were found that indeed were dead, but had been killed and buried elsewhere, so we could cut down on the number of possible decedents. So with that database, we set it up with a search engine that we could, if the pathologists, working over in the morgue, gave us a description of a person, let us say, an unusual injury or a prosthetic device, something that would be a possible feature of identification, we could run through our database and have a printout of the people who would fall within that category, perhaps half a dozen names. Then we could take the records and the ante mortem records that had derived from the relatives families, medical records and so forth, over to the morgue and do a more detailed examination perhaps to pinpoint the person this most closely resembled, thereby making what we were classifying as a tentative identification. In other words, we could say with a fair degree of confidence -- based on experience, I would say with about 95 per cent probability or better -- that, based on this physical description, these remains belonged to that person. Our purpose in making the tentative identifications was that it would facilitate the later process of making positive identification through dental records or X-rays or, primarily, DNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Snow, the process of positive identification is a very much slower process, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is slower and also requires a considerable amount of expertise in that particular area and so those -- some of those identifications have been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The process of tentative identification, how deep -- what percentage of certainty approximately would that run into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, about 95 per cent. Judging from what I could see on the body compared with what the relatives had described, I could say with about 95 per cent probability or better -- 99 per cent probability in a few cases, I would think -- I could say that this was indeed body number such and such, was indeed person number so and so. Before I left Zagreb on November 5th, I believe, 1996, they had been able to identify -- make 51 of these tentative identifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say the identification process, it is by comparing the details in the ante mortem database with the skeletal remains and then from that process, making the tentative identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you are aware, of course, that there was a complete exhumation of the grave by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and that at the end of that, the total number of bodies were -- 200 bodies were recovered from the grave.
