utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The results of the complete exhumation by the Office of the Prosecutor, were they consistent with your initial predictions and information that you had when you first commenced the process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, indeed it confirmed that this was indeed a mass grave. Based on a considerable amount of evidence in the way of bandaged wounds, for example, hospital clothing, it did confirm that at least the majority of these victims had been hospitalised at or around the time of their death, and most of the -- there was clear-cut evidence -- and I am really addressing evidence that should be addressed by the pathologists -- but there was clear-cut evidence of gunshot wounds to the majority of the victims, often multiple gunshot wounds. Of the roughly 51 or exactly 51 tentative identifications I was able to make, they were all indeed people who had been missing from -- listed as missing from the Vukovar hospital, who had not been seen alive from, I believe, November 20th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I have attended to tendering everything that has been shown to Dr. Snow. Subject to that not being the case, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will have only a few very brief questions for this witness. My first question is the following: why did not the exhumation start right away after the first visit at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For one reason, it takes a great deal of time and planning to undertake an exhumation of this magnitude. In our case, we had to recruit scientists from a number of disciplines, not only anthropology, but archaeology, pathology, crime scene specialists and other disciplines, and these kind of personnel are not the kind that are listed in the yellow pages of your phone book. You have to reach out all over the world. In fact, in that team that we fielded in 1993, we had about 15 people and it included colleagues of mine from Argentina, Guatemala, Chile and the United States, so it takes time to plan these things and to implement them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that while contacting your colleagues, you mentioned that you contacted your colleagues, your experts in Zagreb. Did you try to contact or invite other specialists, some specialists from Belgrade, from Yugoslavia, maybe experts from the JNA and was any of them present there? Here I can mention the name of Dr. Stankovic perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We, in our examination, made it very clear to both parties of the conflict, the Serbian and Croatian parties, that this investigation would be conducted by scientists independent of both of them. But at the same time, we to some extent, we had to work with the Croatian -- the people that were collecting the ante mortem database, because they were the ones that were in contact with the families and helping us put that database together. But we did not permit them to be involved in either the exhumation at the site or the examination of the bodies in the morgue. We did have observers. We told both parties that they could be welcomed both to the scene, the site, and to the morgue in Zagreb and they would be welcome as observers. They could ask questions and we would try our best to answer them, but they could not participate in the investigation. Now, in the morgue in Belgrade, we had a very fine elderly gentleman, about my age, and I do not recall his name at the moment, but he is a well known and well thought of pathologist with a reputation well beyond the country. He is well known in Europe and elsewhere. He is Serbian and he was delegated as the Serbian observer. He did -- he made regular visits to the morgue each day and monitored the progress of the work and we tried our best to answer any questions that he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May I know his name? The name of this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am trying to recall his name, sir, but it just does not come to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. No problem. Did you request assistance from Yugoslav authorities, from maybe JNA authorities, to secure the site throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did not myself. That was not my function in this and you would have to ask other people involved in the administrative planning of the exhumation as to what degree of cooperation they asked from the Yugoslavian parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And my last question: I assume that you have seen the complete documentation regarding these 200 bodies, 200 people that ended up at Ovcara. Did you find that some of them were wearing plasters on healthy legs or arms? That it was just a disguise, that they did not have actual wounds or fractures, if you can remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, most of my time during this phase of the investigation, I stayed in the data centre myself working with the database and I would make periodic visits to the morgue. To answer that question, you would have to talk to the pathologists that made the examinations and they may recall cases of that sort that I am not aware of. I am sorry, sir, but I just cannot answer the question because I do not know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no other questions, except exhibit 96 has been tendered, so if it has not, I tender it. That is all now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand there is no objection to the witness being released. Dr. Snow, thank you so much for coming here to give evidence. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: me. (The witness was released)

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness is William Fenrick. I called for him a few moments ago, so he should be outside now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Commander Fenrick, may I ask you to make the solemn declaration, please. COMMANDER WILLIAM FENRICK (affirmed)

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, where are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am currently employed by the Office of the Prosecutor in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And is this your first position with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my second position with the United Nations. At an earlier point in time, I was employed on a part-time basis as a member of a Commission of Experts looking into alleged war crimes in the Former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what were your particular responsibilities with the Commission of Experts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a member of the Commission of Experts, I was specifically also tasked to be the rapporteur on legal issues and rapporteur for on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In this capacity, did you have some role in the planned exhumation of the grave site at Ovcara near Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did indeed. I was not involved in the -- rather, I was involved to a modest degree in the original decision to conduct the excavation, but I was certainly very actively involved at all points subsequent to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And are you aware of why this particular location was selected for exhumation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was believed to be the site where a number of Croatian victims from the Vukovar hospital had been buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And in carrying out this role, were you aware of efforts which had been made prior to the Commission of Experts to exhume the grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding was that the Physicians for Human Rights had made a number of earlier visits to the grave. As to whether or not they had done much more than a preliminary site survey, I am not sure. I do not believe that they had in fact intended to conduct a complete excavation by themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In relation to that issue, have you had an opportunity to review correspondence which was sent by the Regional Council of Slovonia, Baranja and Western Srem to Larry Moore, a police official in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to show the witness a document which I will mark as Prosecutor's exhibit 97. Mr. Fenrick, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what this document relates to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a document which is related to the alleged mass grave and a desire on the part of Dr. Snow and other persons from Physicians for Human Rights to conduct an investigation of the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And who is this letter signed by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This letter is signed by Larry Moore, who, to my recollection, was a --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sorry, can you look on the second page and see who it is signed by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is signed by Milan B Ilic, President of the Regional Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Are you aware of the position that the Regional Council of Slovenia, Baranja and Western Srem has taken in relation to this proposed exhumation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my understanding that this Municipal Council or this Regional Council, rather, was opposed to the excavation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Is that reflected in this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After this initial attempt to conduct an exhumation by Dr. Snow was blocked in 1992, did the Commission of Experts enter into serious efforts to exhume the grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It entered into extremely serious efforts. I made repeated visits to the area itself and also to other parts of the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you relate to the court what transpired during the course of 1993 as you oversaw attempts to exhume the grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will -- if I may, I would like to refer to a chronology of events which was made under my supervision at the time when the incidents occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If that is acceptable to your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first attempt that we made was to in fact conduct a reconnaissance mission to the Vukovar area in March of 1993. The purpose of that mission was to try and determine whether or not an excavation might be practicable, what kind of resources would be needed, what the response of local authorities would be. In March of 1993, I went to the Vukovar area and specifically to the Ovcara site. I was accompanied by a Dr. Snow, among others, some people from Physicians for Human Rights and a small Canadian military team made up of military lawyers and military police. During that particular reconnaissance visit, we were for a short period of time detained by local authorities for taking pictures of the route between Vukovar and Ovcara. We met with various local authorities and particularly with a Colonel Milanovic, who described himself as the Deputy Minister of Defence of the so-called -- he did not use the express "so-called" -- Republic of Serbian Krajina, and at that time we were informed that in order to conduct the excavation, we would have to get the approval of authorities in Knin. We also of course determined that it was necessary to have some fairly substantial resources to conduct the mass grave excavation. The Commission of Experts was essentially made up of a number of law professors and myself and this was not exactly a type of work which we had been used to in the past. It took some time for us both to accumulate the resources to conduct a proper excavation and there were also repeated meetings with a number of local authorities in order to endeavour to obtain approval for conducting the excavation. At various points in time, I visited Belgrade where I met the then Foreign Minister of the RSK. He promised that he would support our efforts to conduct an excavation. At the end of April and in May, I went to Knin and met with, among others, the President of the RSK, Mr. Bjegovic, and he gave us an oral promise that we would be able to conduct the excavation. At a later point in time, we had an exchange of correspondence between the Commission and the administration of the RSK. We were given permission to proceed at the beginning of September. I went to Knin once again and was once again given permission to proceed. Mr. Bjegovic signed letters giving us official authorisation to conduct the excavation. We gradually accumulated the resources that we needed in order to conduct an excavation. We had those resources in Zagreb as of roughly the middle of October of 1993. At that point in time, I once again went to Knin. We discussed several other related issues or issues related to the excavation, as to how we should go ahead, who should participate, whether or not there should be observers, for example, and once again we got written authorisation to conduct the excavation at Ovcara. During the week commencing 17th October 1993, we deployed the various people involved in the excavation to Ovcara, or to the Ovcara area to be more precise. As soon as we arrived in the area, however, we were promptly told that in fact we did not have permission to conduct the excavation. We were compelled to remain at our base camp for a couple of days. We did a little bit of preliminary surface site survey work at the Ovcara site, but then we met once again with Mr. Milanovic, the Deputy Minister of Defence, and we were informed that in fact there had been a decree signed which prohibited us from conducting the excavation for the duration of the conflict. There were some extended discussions at this period of time, but it became quite apparent that it was impracticable for us to conduct the excavation because of a security threat. There was no question that, regardless of the extent of UNPROFOR's control over other sectors that were occupied in Croatia, in Sector East, the Croatian Serbs were in fact by far the most powerful entity there, and I think the UNPROFOR people were somewhat more reserved about assisting us in that particular area as opposed to the kind of assistance we received in other areas. As a result of the opposition of the Croatian Serbs, we gradually over a period of a couple of weeks, deployed the resources that we had sent to the Vukovar and Ovcara area to Sector East where we conducted some additional --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sorry, was that Sector East?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, it was Sector West I should have said, the Pakracka Poljan area where we conducted another mass grave excavation. We did have, after the middle of October, subsequent negotiations with various Croatian Serb authorities. Later in the month of October, the then Chairman of the Commission, Professor Bacuni, and I went to Knin where we were assured -- where we were told, rather, that the problem was that the "government had agreed to us conducting the excavation, but it had been overruled by some Supreme Council of National Defence". At various points in time, we had the impression that there were sort of entities created for the occasion, that no matter what might be approved by the people in Knin, there would always be some either local or "supreme entity" which would override the government's decision. From our point of view, perhaps the most cynical demonstration of lack of cooperation came some time shortly after October when, if I remember correctly, during the year -- during 1993, the last time when it was practicable to conduct an excavation for that year was roughly about the 10th November, and the reason for that was that was roughly the time of year when the snow began to fall. On 16th November, I went back to the Vukovar area, specially to Erdut, where I met with Mr. Hadzic, who at that time was the President of the RSK, with Mr. Niksic, who was the Vice-Chairman of the Regional Council, and with Colonel Milanovic, who was the Deputy Minister of Defence of the RSK. At this time, although in our earlier meetings in the Vukovar area, the strong man was clearly Colonel Milanovic, at this time, during this particular 16th November meeting, President Hadzic was clearly the strong figure. He was very, very supportive of our work. He essentially issued a statement indicating that the RSK authorities agreed to cooperate and give their approval for us conducting the excavation, and they did. However, bear in mind that of course we had now reached the snow season, so the excavation would be allowed to be carried on in the following year, beginning March or April. President Hadzic was extremely cooperative. The only problem was, as all who were there were well aware, the RSK had scheduled elections for December of 1993 and President Hadzic was not running for re-election. So the promise was purely a paper promise since President Hadzic did not run for re-election. His statement that we would be allowed to proceed at the beginning of the next year or at the beginning of the digging season in the next year in March or April was of no value whatsoever. In fact, we did not go back and dig during 1994 or throughout the length of the Commission of Experts' existence and it expired in June of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, you mentioned that at this meeting with Goran Hadzic that Chancellor Niksic was also present. I would like to show you a document, which I will mark as Prosecutor's exhibit 98. I request you identify this document, please. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this document very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And can you indicate to the court what is set forth in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Essentially, this document indicates that the National Parliament of the Republic of Serbian Krajina refuses to authorise the Commission of Experts to conduct an excavation at the Ovcara site until a political solution is found to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would tender this exhibit. Exhibit 98. Mr. Fenrick, at the conclusion of your work with the Commission of Experts, did you participate in the compilation of a final report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And in connection with that, did you draft a portion which related to the attempts to exhume the mass grave at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would show the witness an exhibit I will mark now as Prosecutor's exhibit 99. (Handed). I would ask if you could identify this item.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a portion of the final report which I drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what does this portion relate to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This portion relates to the investigation of grave sites at Ovcara near Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And which paragraphs by numbers are included in this relevant portion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paragraphs 265 through 276 inclusive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would tender this as Prosecutor's exhibit 99.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When the mandate of the Commission of Experts concluded, did you subsequently enter employment with the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 2nd August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In this position, did you participate in discussions relative to the Tribunal undertaking the exhumation of the Ovcara grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And as such, did you become aware of a letter which was sent by Deputy Prosecutor Graham Blewitt to Juros Fundak, an official in the government in the so-called Republic of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to show a document to Mr. Fenrick, which will be marked as Prosecutor's exhibit 100. Can you identify this document? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It is a document sent by Graham Blewitt, the Deputy Prosecutor, to Mr. Juros Fundak of the Serbian Krajina administration in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What is requested in this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a request that certain members of the Prosecutor's staff be allowed to visit Knin to discuss exhumation of the bodies allegedly buried at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Are you aware of a letter which was sent by Mr. Fundak in response to Mr. Blewitt's request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would like to show you now a document which we will mark as Prosecutor's exhibit 101. (Handed). Can you identify this item?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a reply from Mr. Juros Fundak to the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What does this letter indicate in response to Mr. Blewitt's request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It adopts an extremely negative approach and essentially ignores the issue and merely suggests that communications with the so-called Republic of Serbia Krajina should be conducted in a more official fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would tender these last two documents as exhibits 100 and 101. Mr. Fenrick, are you aware if the Serbian authorities in the Vukovar region ever acquiesced in allowing the exhumation to go forward?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, they did not acquiesce at any point in time when they controlled the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was the grave ever exhumed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the grave was exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you know how this was accomplished without the cooperation of the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was only accomplished at a subsequent point in time when the effective power in the area was in fact exercised by UNTAES, the UN transitional administrative -- administration for Eastern Slovonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I have no further questions. I do not believe I have tendered exhibit 97, so if I failed to do that, I will do that now. Sorry, I believe it has been tendered. I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, I just have one question. You spoke of your contacts. In response to the questions of the Prosecutor, you spoke about your contacts with the local Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who do you mean by that? Who are the local Serb authorities? The authorities of the Republic of Serbia Krajina self-styled or not self-styled or the municipal authorities. The President of the Municipality, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main person at any meeting that I attended other than the one in late November of 1993 was always Colonel Milanovic who was an authority for the so-called republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you have any kind of contact? Do you know who was the President of the Municipality of Vukovar throughout this period during which you were talking to these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you have any contact with someone from the Municipality of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not directly to my knowledge. There were always --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am asking a direct question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. Mr. Fenrick should be allowed to answer the question in full, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, can you rephrase?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I did not understand, sorry. I am sorry, I did not understand the question; that is why I asked. The question was: did you talk at a lower level than that of the Republic of Srpska Krajina? Did you talk to the President of the Municipality or someone like that at municipal level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were always additional people at the meetings, but the -- effective head of any meeting that I attended was always Colonel Molanovic. That is the meetings in the Erdut or Vukovar area, except for the meeting of the 16th which was headed by Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That will be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At the time that you were detained by the police in Vukovar, did you meet a delegation which was represented to you as being from the local administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but to be honest, I could not identify and cannot recollect the names of any of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I do not really have a question, but just a small clarification. When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was in March of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No further questions? I assume there is no objection to Commander Fenrick being excused? Commander Fenrick, thank you so much for coming here to give evidence. You may now be excused. (The witness was released)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we do not have any further witnesses for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct your Honour. At this time, we were prepared to show a videotape which gives an overview of the Ovcara exhumation. It is an approximately 30 minute videotape and, assuming that all of our admissions are agreed to with the Defence, that would conclude all of our evidence in relation to the exhumation. If however there is no agreement, then we would be required to put on additional witnesses, but assuming that that can be reached, this will be our final piece of evidence in that regard. I believe the video is ready to proceed at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The Defence said that they are not disputing any of this, so why manipulate with it? (A video was played to the court).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have no further evidence for today, your Honour. The next witness will be available to be called on Thursday morning, so we have no evidence for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What is the estimated length of his examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it will be relatively lengthy. It is possible that it may go as long as three hours and perhaps even more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That means we better start at 8.30 on Thursday. Yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I assume that you are talking about the witness whose name has been listed in the order, for whom you have requested a closed session? I am not going to mention his name, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct, but it will be an open session in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: An open session? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to draw the attention of the court to something. I have received a statement of this person, the witness, and there is nothing in that statement about Dokmanovic, Vukovar or the year of 1991, November 1991. Therefore, it has nothing to do with this case and what I have read in the statement pertained to Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I would like that an additional statement be taken from that witness so that I would be notified of the contents of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt, but perhaps the discussion of this matter, we might move into closed session, because I think there are some issues that pertain to other cases, which we must address in a closed session. I apologise for interrupting Mr. Fila, but I think in order to safeguard the witness that would be the preferable course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that we should do so right away?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is fine, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I may assist you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am sorry, but it is private session rather than closed session. Maybe that is easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I assist you? It will not be necessary to lose any additional time. It would simply be very valuable if a statement could be taken from that gentleman. Otherwise I am opposed to the calling of this witness because I have no idea on what he is going to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Fila, I see your point, but the Prosecutor has just suggested that we discuss a few issues in a closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I believe the correct title for it would be a private session, under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It takes only one or two minutes to move on to a private session. (Private session)
